content: Crohn's disease (CD) is a chronic inflammatory condition of the gastrointestinal tract, characterized by alternating periods of active disease and symptom-free remission. Probiotics, which are live microorganisms thought to confer health benefits, have been investigated as a potential alternative therapy to prevent relapse in patients with CD. To evaluate the effectiveness of probiotics in maintaining remission in CD, a systematic review was conducted. Multiple databases were searched, including the Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews, MEDLINE, EMBASE, and others, covering studies up to 2005. Experts in the field were also contacted to identify unpublished data. The review included randomized controlled trials (RCTs) that assessed probiotic therapy for this purpose. Two independent reviewers extracted data and assessed the methodological quality of the studies. The primary outcome was the relative risk (RR) of relapse after maintenance treatment, with 95% confidence intervals (CI). Seven small studies were identified, but they varied in terms of the specific probiotics tested, study quality, and medication regimens used. Due to these differences, no studies were combined for statistical analysis. The results showed no statistically significant benefit of the probiotic E. coli Nissle in reducing the risk of relapse compared to placebo (RR 0.43, 95% CI 0.15 to 1.20). Similarly, Lactobacillus GG did not demonstrate a significant benefit in preventing relapse after either surgically-induced remission (RR 1.58, 95% CI 0.30 to 8.40) or medically-induced remission (RR 0.83, 95% CI 0.25 to 2.80). When probiotics were compared to standard maintenance therapies such as aminosalicylates or azathioprine, no significant benefit was observed (RR 0.67, 95% CI 0.13 to 3.30). In fact, in one study, Lactobacillus GG was associated with adverse events. In pediatric patients, there was no significant difference between Lactobacillus GG and placebo in reducing the risk of relapse (RR 1.85, 95% CI 0.77 to 4.40). A small study using the yeast Saccharomyces boulardii showed a non-significant trend favoring the probiotic combined with reduced maintenance therapy over standard maintenance therapy alone (RR 0.17, 95% CI 0.02 to 1.23). The authors concluded that there is no evidence to support the use of probiotics for maintaining remission in Crohn's disease. All included studies had small sample sizes, which may have limited their ability to detect significant differences if they existed. Larger, well-designed trials are needed to determine whether probiotics have any role in the management of Crohn's disease.
